brief.userPrompt: Every POS terminal in the airport goes dark two minutes after the IT Manager's emergency firewall rule, while a real SSH scan and a vendor firmware push make a cyberattack and a supply-chain compromise look equally plausible.
learningObjectives: Follow evidence instead of assumptions when diagnosing an outage (diagnostic rigor)
Resist confirmation bias when real but unrelated events make an attack theory feel true
Identify change management failures (self-approval, no peer review, no post-change verification) as systemic root causes
Communicate under uncertainty without prematurely declaring a cyberattack
Balance accountability and blame when the cause is an internal error
constraints: puzzle-driven: three theories, two red herrings, one correct answer

overview.theme: Incident misidentification. Confirmation bias. Change management failures. What happens when the "attacker" is sitting in the room and doesn't know it.
overview.threat: Not an attack: IT Manager Jordan Kelley wrote an emergency firewall rule (CM-2026-0087, 09:45) meant to block 185.220.0.0/16 but set Source Zone and Source Address to "any" with the Retail VLAN (10.1.40.0/24) as destination, at position 3 above the inter-VLAN allow rules. Two red herrings compete: real failed SSH scanning from 185.220.101.34 at 2 AM and a RetailLink firmware push at 9:30 AM.
overview.operationalImpact: All 47 retail tenants are cash-only, Concourse B food court FIDS displays are dark, gate management terminals and landside check-in kiosks are intermittent, and airlines face delayed departures, with media and social attention building around a presumed cyberattack.
overview.targetAudience: Airport Operations, IT/Cybersecurity, Public Information (PIO), Security, Legal & Compliance.

objectives.name: Diagnostic Rigor
objectives.text: Can the IT team follow evidence instead of assumptions? Do they read the actual firewall rule, or do they chase the more exciting cyberattack theory?

objectives.name: Confirmation Bias
objectives.text: The exercise is designed to exploit the team's natural tendency to see what they expect to see. External scanning + vendor issues = "it must be an attack." Do they resist that pull?

objectives.name: Change Management
objectives.text: The root cause is a process failure — self-approval, no peer review, no post-change verification. Does the team identify the systemic issues or just blame the individual?

objectives.name: Crisis Communication Under Uncertainty
objectives.text: Can PIO manage media and passengers without prematurely declaring a cyberattack that turns out to be a typo?

objectives.name: Accountability vs. Blame
objectives.text: The Jordan Kelley question. Fire him or fix the system that let him make the mistake?

roles.name: Airport Operations (Command)
roles.description: 47 retail tenants can't process card transactions. Passengers are standing in lines with no way to pay. Airlines are reporting check-in kiosk failures. Manage the operational fallout while IT figures out the cause.
standingOrders: Triage: Which systems are down and what's the passenger impact?
Communicate: Tenant liaison, airline ops, passenger messaging.
Cash Ops: Coordinate with tenants on cash-only procedures and ATM availability.

roles.name: IT & Cybersecurity (Lead)
roles.description: Three theories. One answer. The evidence is in the firewall logs, the SIEM, the change management system, the vendor communication, and the network traffic data. Eliminate two theories and confirm one. Then fix it.
standingOrders: Investigate: Firewall rule analysis, SIEM log review, vendor contact, change log audit.
Contain: If it's an attack, isolate. If it's a vendor issue, roll back. If it's internal, revert.
Communicate: Keep the room informed. Don't disappear into the logs — translate for the non-IT teams.

roles.name: Public Information Officer
roles.description: Passengers are already posting on social media: "NCIA card readers down — can't buy coffee." One person has tweeted "Are we under cyberattack??" You don't know the answer yet. Say something without saying the wrong thing.
standingOrders: Monitor: Track social media in real time.
Draft: Prepare statements for three scenarios (attack, vendor failure, internal error).
Hold: Do NOT confirm a cyberattack until IT has confirmed it. Premature disclosure is irreversible.

roles.name: Security, Legal & Compliance
roles.description: If this is a cyberattack, PCI-DSS notification requirements may be triggered. TSA may need to be informed depending on scope. If payment card data was compromised, the state Attorney General's office has a 72-hour notification window. But if it's NOT an attack, none of that applies. Be ready for both.
standingOrders: Assess: Is there any indication that payment card data was accessed or exfiltrated?
Standby: Prepare notification templates for TSA, PCI council, state AG — but do NOT send.
Coordinate: If law enforcement is needed, what's the trigger?

phases.title: Briefing
phases.goal: Present all three theories equally. Do NOT hint at the answer. Let IT study the Evidence Packet.

phases.title: Chase the Theories
phases.goal: The team pursues all three theories. Each inject reinforces one theory before the next inject undermines it. The evidence oscillates — keeping the team uncertain.

phases.title: The Evidence Converges
phases.goal: Theory A collapses. Theory C gains traction. The team reads the actual firewall rule and finds the errors. The "aha" moment.

phases.title: The Reckoning
phases.goal: Root cause analysis. Change management failures. Process improvements. And the hardest question: what do you do about Jordan Kelley?

phases.title: Debrief / Hot Wash
phases.goal: 3-Up / 3-Down. Focus on: confirmation bias, change management, and the tension between accountability and blame.

msel.event: STARTEX. Distribute Player Briefing Packet. Give Network Evidence Packet to IT only. Present all three theories equally. Do NOT hint at the answer. The team should feel genuinely uncertain about which theory is correct.
msel.expectedAction: Teams organize. IT begins reviewing evidence. All teams should note the dual-clock: investigate AND manage the operational impact simultaneously.

msel.event: Airport's tenant coordinator calls: "I'm getting hammered by vendors. SkyLounge, Concourse News, the duty-free shop — every single one is cash-only. Passengers are furious. The Harbor Coffee in Concourse A has a line out the door and they can't process a single card. I need a timeline for restoration. What do I tell 47 tenants?"
msel.expectedAction: Ops must manage the operational fallout NOW — independent of the investigation. Options: coordinate cash-only signage, direct passengers to ATMs, contact airline clubs about POS workarounds. The tenant coordinator needs answers, not "we're investigating."

msel.event: Phone call from RetailLink support: "We heard your terminals are down. We did push firmware v4.2.1 at 9:30 this morning — it's a routine PCI compliance patch. We've checked our end and the update completed successfully on all 47 terminals. The terminals are online — they're just not reaching your payment gateway. This looks like a network issue on YOUR side, not a terminal issue on ours. Also, FYI — we flagged unusual API queries against our cloud portal yesterday from an IP we didn't recognize. We reported it to our security team. Unrelated, probably, but I wanted to mention it."
msel.expectedAction: ELIMINATES THEORY B — partially. The firmware update didn't change terminal network settings. The terminals are online. The problem is between the terminals and the gateway — that's network, not vendor. But the "unusual API queries" comment re-fuels Theory A (external attack). IT should note: the vendor issue and the outage may be coincidental, not causal.

msel.event: IT reports on SIEM analysis: "We found the SSH scanning from last night — 185.220.101.34. Three failed login attempts against the firewall between 2:00 and 2:15 AM. All three failed — wrong credentials. No access was gained. But here's the thing: that IP is from a known scanning botnet flagged in CISA advisory TI-2026-0312. Someone was actively probing our firewall 7 hours before the outage. Coincidence? We also see that Jordan Kelley wrote a firewall rule this morning at 09:45 specifically to block that IP range. The rule is in the change log as CM-2026-0087. We should look at that rule."
msel.expectedAction: This introduces the critical timeline: scan at 2 AM → Kelley writes blocking rule at 9:45 → outage at 9:47. The IT team should now want to inspect the actual rule. If they pivot to reading the firewall rule, they're on the right track. If they stay focused on the SSH scanning, they're still chasing Theory A.

msel.event: PIO monitors social media: trending posts include "@NCIAirport card readers are all down — anyone else stuck paying cash?" and "Is NCIA under cyberattack?? Nothing is working." A local reporter has DM'd the airport's account: "We're hearing reports of a major system outage at NCIA. Is this a cyberattack? We're going live at noon. Comment?"
msel.expectedAction: PIO must decide: what do you say? You don't know the cause yet. If you say "we're under investigation for a cyberattack" and it turns out to be a typo, that headline lives forever. If you say "it's a minor technical issue" and it IS an attack, you look like you covered it up. The correct statement is neutral: "We're experiencing a temporary system issue affecting some retail terminals. We're working to restore service and will provide updates as available."

msel.event: IT reports on the firewall rule CM-2026-0087: "We pulled the actual rule from the running config. It was supposed to block inbound traffic from 185.220.0.0/16. But that's not what it says. Source Zone is set to 'any' — not 'Untrust.' That means it applies to ALL zones, including internal VLANs. Source Address is set to 'any' — not 185.220.0.0/16. That means ALL source addresses. Destination is 10.1.40.0/24 — the Retail VLAN. Action is DENY. Position 3 — above the inter-VLAN allow rules. This rule says: deny ALL traffic from ANYWHERE going to the Retail VLAN. That's not a targeted block on an external threat. That's a kill switch on our Retail VLAN. And it was put there by Jordan Kelley at 9:45 this morning. Two minutes before every POS terminal went dark." (Silence.)
msel.expectedAction: THE ANSWER. Theory C confirmed. The outage was caused by an overly broad firewall rule written by the IT Manager himself. Three errors: wrong source zone, wrong source address, and the rule was placed above the allow rules in the policy order. This is the emotional pivot. The team expected an attacker. They got a typo. Let the room absorb it. Then someone will ask: "Can we just delete the rule and fix it?" (Yes — but that's not the end of the exercise.)

msel.event: DECISION: "The fix is straightforward — delete rule TI-2026-0312-Block and traffic between VLAN 10 and VLAN 40 will be restored instantly. Do you delete it now?" But wait: the original threat was real. 185.220.0.0/16 WAS scanning your firewall last night. If you delete the rule entirely, you're removing the protection Kelley was trying to add. If you rewrite it correctly, you have to get it right THIS time. Option A: Delete the rule. Restore service immediately. Deal with the threat intel later. Option B: Rewrite the rule correctly (Source Zone: Untrust, Source Address: 185.220.0.0/16, Dest: any) and apply the corrected version. Takes 5-10 more minutes. Option C: Delete the rule AND apply a temporary block on 185.220.101.34 (the specific scanning IP) as a targeted measure while a proper rule is designed and peer-reviewed.
msel.expectedAction: Option C is the best answer — it restores service AND addresses the real threat with a narrow, targeted block. But any option that restores service is acceptable. The real question is: does the IT team want someone to peer-review the corrected rule before it's applied? (They should. That's the change management lesson.)

msel.event: Skyline station manager calls: "Our check-in kiosks were timing out for 45 minutes. I've got 200 passengers who couldn't use self-service check-in. My agents are processing them manually and we're looking at a 40-minute delay on three departures. I need a root cause analysis by end of day, and I need assurance this won't happen again. Was this a cyberattack?"
msel.expectedAction: Ops must decide what to tell the airline. The truth is embarrassing: it was a misconfigured firewall rule — your own IT team's mistake. But the airline needs a candid answer. If they find out later that you misrepresented the cause, trust is broken. The correct approach: "The outage was caused by an internal configuration error that has been corrected. It was not a cyberattack. We are implementing additional controls to prevent recurrence."

msel.event: Reporter calls PIO: "We're going live at noon with the NCIA outage story. We have multiple passenger reports that the airport's payment systems were down for over an hour. One source is telling us it was a cyberattack. Can you confirm or deny?"
msel.expectedAction: PIO now faces the hardest version of this question. They know it WASN'T a cyberattack. But saying "it was our own mistake" is embarrassing. Saying "no comment" lets the cyberattack narrative run. The correct approach: issue a statement that's candid without being self-flagellating. "At approximately 9:47 AM, a configuration error in our network infrastructure caused a temporary disruption to retail payment systems. The issue was identified and corrected within [X] minutes. This was not a cyberattack. We are reviewing our change management procedures to prevent recurrence."

msel.event: ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS. The facilitator walks through the failure chain: 1. Real threat detected (SSH scanning) — appropriate concern. 2. Kelley decides to write a blocking rule — reasonable response. 3. The rule was self-approved — NCIA policy allows emergency threat mitigation without peer review. 4. Three errors in the rule: wrong source zone, wrong source address, rule position above allow rules. 5. No post-change verification — Kelley was called to a meeting and didn't check. 6. The outage was detected in 2 minutes — but cause identification took [however long it took the team]. "Where did the process fail? Was it the person, the policy, or both?"
msel.expectedAction: This is the systems-thinking discussion. Kelley made a mistake, but the system ALLOWED the mistake: no peer review, no automated validation, no post-change testing requirement, no firewall rule syntax checking. The question is not "fire Kelley" — it's "what controls would have caught this before it went live?"

msel.event: THE JORDAN KELLEY QUESTION. The facilitator asks directly: "Jordan Kelley is your IT Manager. He wrote the rule. He self-approved it. He didn't verify it. He crashed your retail network for [X] minutes. 47 tenants couldn't process transactions. Airlines delayed flights. You may have PCI reporting obligations. The media called. Do you discipline him? Fire him? Or do you recognize that the system allowed a single person to make a change with no review, no validation, and no verification — and that if Kelley hadn't made this mistake, someone else eventually would have? What do you do with Jordan?"
msel.expectedAction: This is the exercise's emotional peak. Some will want to fire him. Others will defend him. The best answer is nuanced: Kelley made a mistake, but the organization failed to prevent it. A blame-free culture that focuses on process improvement is more resilient than one that fires the person who made the error. But there IS accountability for skipping post-change verification. Let the room argue. The argument IS the exercise.

msel.event: PROCESS IMPROVEMENT. Each team addresses their area: — IT: Mandatory peer review for all firewall changes (no self-approval). Automated rule validation (syntax check against known-good patterns). Mandatory post-change verification checklist. Firewall rule change staging environment. Alert-on-deny-rule creation. — Ops: Retail outage playbook — what to do in the first 5 minutes when POS goes down. Cash-only signage pre-staged. ATM location communication. Airline notification protocol. — PIO: Pre-drafted holding statements for system outages (attack vs. error vs. unknown). Social media monitoring escalation triggers. — Legal: When does a network outage trigger PCI notification? When does it NOT? What's the threshold? (Answer: if no card data was compromised, PCI notification is not required — but you need to confirm no data was exposed.)
msel.expectedAction: Push for specifics. "When does the peer review policy go into effect? Tomorrow? Next quarter? What does the staging environment look like? Who reviews emergency changes at 2 AM?"

msel.event: ENDEX. 3-Up / 3-Down, followed by key discussion questions: 1. Which theory did you pursue first? Why? How long before you pivoted? 2. Did you WANT it to be a cyberattack? Why is that instinct dangerous? 3. How long did it take to read the actual firewall rule? Could you have found it faster? 4. What would you tell the airlines? The media? The board? 5. Jordan Kelley — what did you decide? Would you feel different if it was you?
msel.expectedAction: Team reflects. Facilitator captures lessons. Exercise complete.

metrics.name: Diagnostic Accuracy
metrics.fail: Team declared a cyberattack without confirming. Never read the firewall rule.
metrics.pass: Team eventually identified Theory C as correct after working through the evidence.
metrics.excellence: IT identified the firewall rule errors independently from the Evidence Packet, correlated the 09:45 change with the 09:47 outage, and eliminated A and B with specific evidence.

metrics.name: Operational Management
metrics.fail: Team focused entirely on investigation. Tenants, airlines, and passengers were ignored.
metrics.pass: Ops coordinated cash-only procedures and communicated with tenants and airlines.
metrics.excellence: Ops had cash-only signage deployed within 10 minutes, directed passengers to ATMs, coordinated with airline ops on kiosk workarounds, and gave tenants a restoration timeline.

metrics.name: Crisis Comms
metrics.fail: PIO confirmed a cyberattack prematurely, or gave "no comment" to all inquiries.
metrics.pass: PIO issued a holding statement that didn't confirm or deny attack.
metrics.excellence: PIO had differentiated statements pre-drafted for all three scenarios, issued accurate correction once cause was confirmed, and proactively managed the media narrative.

metrics.name: Process Improvement
metrics.fail: Team focused on blaming Kelley. Didn't address systemic issues.
metrics.pass: Team identified the self-approval policy and lack of peer review as contributing factors.
metrics.excellence: Team produced a comprehensive improvement plan: mandatory peer review, automated rule validation, post-change verification checklist, staging environment, and a nuanced accountability approach for Kelley that balances consequences with culture.

objectiveCapabilities.why: The objective tests whether the IT team relies on actual network evidence—specifically the firewall rule configuration—rather than assumptions about external threats, which is central to cybersecurity's role in protecting and restoring electronic systems and verifying configurations.

The objective requires the team to assess the true nature of the threat by analyzing logs, traffic data, and rule configurations, which is a core function of situational assessment in response operations.

The objective tests whether the team uses verified data from multiple sources—SIEM logs, vendor reports, and network traffic—to counteract preconceived notions, which aligns with intelligence and information sharing's role in ensuring accurate threat assessment.
The team must continuously reassess the threat landscape using objective evidence to avoid being misled by red herrings, a key aspect of situational assessment.
The objective focuses on identifying systemic flaws in change procedures, which falls under planning's role in developing and maintaining processes that prevent recurrence of failures.
The team must assess the risk of unreviewed changes and identify gaps in risk controls, which is central to managing protection programs and activities.
The objective tests whether the PIO delivers timely, accurate, and actionable information to the public under uncertainty, which is the core function of public information and warning.

The decision to fix the system rather than fire the individual reflects a planning mindset focused on long-term resilience, process improvement, and preventing future failures through structured, repeatable procedures.

hotwash.methodDescription: 3-Up / 3-Down, followed by key discussion questions. Focus on: confirmation bias, change management, and the tension between accountability and blame.

questions.text: You had real SSH scanning, a real vendor update, and a real firewall change. Two of those were red herrings. Which theory did you chase first — and was it because of evidence or instinct?
The rule was applied at 9:45. The outage started at 9:47. That's a 2-minute correlation. How long did it take you to make that connection?
Kelley approved his own change under the emergency threat mitigation policy. Should ANY firewall change be self-approved? What about at 2 AM when nobody else is available?
Kelley didn't test after applying the rule. If he had pinged one POS terminal from the Server VLAN, he'd have caught it in 30 seconds. Should post-change verification be mandatory and automated?
In aviation, we have just culture — we don't punish good-faith mistakes, but we hold people accountable for reckless behavior. Was Kelley's mistake a good-faith error or reckless? Where's the line?
If PIO had said 'cyberattack' at noon and you found out it was a typo at 12:30, could you undo that headline? What does premature disclosure cost?

assumptions: The exercise is conducted in a no-fault learning environment where participants are encouraged to explore decisions without fear of real-world consequences.
The scenario is plausible, and events occur as they are presented—no external knowledge or hindsight is permitted.
Players respond in accordance with existing plans, policies, and procedures as documented in the referenced materials.
The SimCell operates all external systems (vendors, tenants, media, mutual aid) and delivers injects via paper and screen as needed.
Time jumps between modules reflect the passage of real-world time, but players only experience events as they are delivered.
artificialities: Time jumps between modules represent the passage of real-world time, but players only experience events as they are delivered.
The SimCell plays all external actors (vendors, tenants, media, partner agencies) and simulates their communications and actions.
Systems named in the plans (e.g., Retail VLAN, Firewall Rule CM-2026-0087) are simulated and not physically accessed.
Injects are delivered via paper and screen, not live calls or emails.
The root cause is hidden until the final inject—players must discover it through evidence and analysis.

modules.narrativeMd:
It is 09:50. The emergency operations center (EOC) is activated for a tabletop exercise. All roles are present: Airport Operations (OPS), IT & Cybersecurity (IT), Public Information Officer (PIO), and Security, Legal & Compliance (LEGAL). The facilitator has distributed the Player Briefing Packet and provided the Network Evidence Packet exclusively to IT. No prior context has been given about the nature of the incident. The team is instructed to review the materials and prepare for an emerging situation.

The initial alert is not yet active. The team has not yet received any injects. They are in a state of readiness, awaiting the first signal of a potential system failure. The environment is calm, but the stage is set for a cascading infrastructure issue affecting the airport’s point-of-sale (POS) systems and terminal operations.
keyIssues: IT must begin diagnosing a network failure without knowing its true cause.
The team must resist jumping to conclusions about a cyberattack based on preliminary evidence.
Ops must prepare to manage tenant and airline concerns before any incident is confirmed.
PIO must anticipate media and passenger reactions, even before a formal declaration.
Legal must begin assessing potential compliance implications, including PCI reporting thresholds.

discussionQuestions.text: IT: Based on the initial evidence packet, what are the three most likely root causes of the POS outage? How do you prioritize your diagnostic steps?

modules.narrativeMd:
It is 10:00. The first inject arrives: the airport’s tenant coordinator calls, reporting that all 47 retail terminals are now cash-only. Passengers are furious, lines are forming, and the duty-free shop cannot process any transactions. The airport’s payment systems are down.

Two minutes later, the RetailLink vendor confirms they pushed a routine firmware update at 9:30 AM. Their terminals are online, but they are not reaching the airport’s payment gateway. The vendor notes unusual API queries from a foreign IP, which they flagged to their security team.

Then, IT reports on a SIEM alert: an IP from a known botnet scanned the firewall between 2:00 and 2:15 AM. The scan was unsuccessful. But the same IP was blocked by a new firewall rule written by Jordan Kelley at 9:45 AM—just minutes before the outage began. The team is now considering three competing theories: a vendor-induced network failure, a cyberattack, or a misconfigured internal change.

The media is beginning to react. Social media is trending: "@NCIAirport card readers are all down — anyone else stuck paying cash?" A local reporter has sent a direct message: "We're hearing reports of a major system outage at NCIA. Is this a cyberattack? We're going live at noon. Comment?"
keyIssues: The team is being pulled toward a cyberattack narrative based on scanning activity and vendor anomalies.
IT must resist confirmation bias and verify the actual firewall rule, not just trust the change log.
Ops must manage rising pressure from tenants and airlines while evidence remains ambiguous.
PIO must respond to media inquiries without confirming a cyberattack, even under pressure.
Legal must begin assessing whether a data breach occurred, even as the cause remains unknown.

discussionQuestions.text: IT: You’ve found a firewall rule (CM-2026-0087) that was self-approved by Jordan Kelley to block the scanning IP. Do you trust the rule as written, or do you investigate its actual configuration?

modules.narrativeMd:
It is 10:30. The IT team has pulled the actual firewall configuration. They discover that the rule written by Jordan Kelley to block the scanning IP (185.220.101.34) was incorrectly configured in three critical ways: the source zone was set to 'any' instead of 'Untrust', the source address was 'any' instead of 185.220.0.0/16, and it was positioned above the inter-VLAN allow rules. This rule, meant to block external traffic, instead blocks all traffic to the Retail VLAN (10.1.40.0/24), including internal traffic from the POS workstations.

The rule is not a targeted block. It is a kill switch. It was applied at 9:45 AM, two minutes before the POS terminals went dark. The scanning was real, but the response was catastrophic. The team now understands: the outage was not caused by an external attack, but by a misconfiguration made in response to a real threat.

The silence in the room is palpable. The evidence has converged. The team must now decide how to restore service—and whether to delete the rule, rewrite it, or apply a temporary fix while a proper rule is peer-reviewed.
keyIssues: The team must now read and interpret the actual firewall rule, not just trust the change log.
The root cause is now clear: a self-approved, unverified rule with three critical errors.
The team must choose between immediate restoration and a safer, slower fix.
The media and stakeholders will demand answers—especially after they’ve heard a cyberattack theory.
Legal must now confirm whether the outage constitutes a data breach, even if no data was compromised.

discussionQuestions.text: IT: You have identified three errors in the firewall rule. What is your immediate action to restore service? What are the risks of each option?

modules.narrativeMd:
It is 11:00. The root cause has been confirmed: a real threat was detected (SSH scanning), but the response—Jordan Kelley’s firewall rule—was self-approved, unverified, and incorrectly configured. The rule blocked all traffic to the Retail VLAN, not just from the scanning IP.

The team now faces the systemic failure: a policy that allows self-approval of emergency changes, but no peer review, no verification, and no staging environment. The error was not a personal failure—it was a process failure. The same mistake could have been made by anyone.

The facilitator poses the central question: Jordan Kelley is responsible for the outage. He made a critical error under pressure. Do you fire him? Discipline him? Or do you recognize that the system allowed a single person to make a change with no oversight, and that if Kelley hadn’t made this mistake, someone else eventually would have?

The team must now decide on a course of action—not just for Jordan, but for the entire organization. They must also begin to design process improvements to prevent recurrence.
keyIssues: The team must confront the tension between accountability and systemic improvement.
The root cause is not the individual, but the process: self-approval, no verification, no staging.
The team must decide whether to fire Jordan Kelley, or to fix the system that enabled his error.
Process improvements must be designed across IT, Ops, and Legal.
The media will demand answers—especially if the team blames a single person.

discussionQuestions.text: IT: What changes would you implement to prevent a similar firewall misconfiguration in the future? What role should peer review and automated validation play?

modules.narrativeMd:
It is 11:30. The exercise has concluded. The team has identified the root cause: a misconfigured firewall rule that blocked all traffic to the Retail VLAN. The error was made by Jordan Kelley, but the system allowed it—no peer review, no verification, no staging.

The team has agreed on process improvements: mandatory peer review for all firewall changes, automated rule validation, a staging environment, and a post-change verification checklist. They have also developed pre-drafted media statements, updated the Retail Outage Playbook, and clarified the PCI reporting threshold.

The final inject is delivered: a 3-Up / 3-Down debrief. The team reflects on their journey: which theory they pursued first, how long it took to read the actual firewall rule, and whether they wanted it to be a cyberattack. They discuss how confirmation bias led them to suspect an attack, and how the pressure to act fast made them overlook the simplest explanation.

The final questions linger: What would you have said to the board? To the airlines? To Jordan Kelley, if he were in the room?
keyIssues: The team must reflect on how confirmation bias influenced their initial response.
The team must assess how long it took to read and trust the actual firewall rule.
The team must decide whether to blame Jordan or fix the system that allowed his error.
The team must evaluate whether their crisis communication strategy was effective under uncertainty.
The team must confront the emotional weight of the Jordan Kelley decision: would they feel differently if it were them?

discussionQuestions.text: IT: How long did it take to read the actual firewall rule? Could you have found it faster? What would you do differently in a real incident?
